messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Public Defender
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 70

**Patient Vignette: Mr. L.**  

Mr. L. is a 68-year-old South Eastern Asian man, a retired public defender who now works part-time as a legal consultant. He has been widowed for six years. He presents with a haunted stillness, his hands often folded in his lap, his gaze fixed on a point just beyond the window. He speaks slowly, as if each word must be excavated from deep earth.  

The event that shattered his world occurred three years ago. His youngest daughter, a journalist, was covering a protest in a city he had once fled as a refugee. She was caught in a stampede during a police crackdown. Mr. L. received the call at 2:17 a.m. He remembers the number on the caller ID, the way the digits seemed to burn into his retina. He remembers the voice of a stranger saying, “Your daughter has been injured. She is in surgery.” He remembers the 14-hour flight, the sterile hospital hallways, the moment a doctor in blue scrubs approached him with a face that already held the answer. She died on the operating table. Internal bleeding. He never saw her body. The authorities said it was too unstable.  

In the months that followed, Mr. L. did not cry. He continued to show up at the courthouse, arguing motions, cross-examining witnesses. He was praised for his composure. But inside, a circuit had been severed. He began to see his daughter’s face in the faces of young women on the street. He would freeze in the grocery store, staring at a bag of jasmine rice, because she used to cook it on Sundays. He stopped answering phone calls from his other children. He stopped cooking altogether.  

Now, three years later, the world feels like a series of landmines. A news report about a protest sends his heart into a gallop. The smell of antiseptic in a doctor’s office makes his stomach clench. He has not entered a hospital since that day. He avoids the airport entirely, driving three hours out of his way to see a client rather than take a short flight. He keeps a small notebook in his pocket, and when the images come—her face, the phone call, the doctor’s scrubs—he writes the date and time and a single word: *later*. He tells himself he will process it later. But later never comes.  

His sleep is a ruin. He wakes at 2:17 a.m. every night, drenched in sweat, convinced he has heard the phone ring. He has checked his phone so many times that the screen is cracked from his grip. During the day, he is easily startled. A car backfiring on the street sends him to the floor. A colleague touching his shoulder at a meeting causes him to flinch and snap, “Don’t.” He has lost two consulting contracts because of what partners called his “unpredictable temper.”  

He has not touched his daughter’s room. The door is closed, a seal on a tomb. He cannot bring himself to donate her clothes, her books, her camera. He tells himself he is keeping them for her son—his grandson—but the boy lives in another country and they have not spoken since the funeral.  

The most painful symptom is the guilt. Mr. L. was a public defender for forty years. He built a career on arguing for the innocent, on believing the system could be made right. But he could not save his own daughter. He replays the night in his mind, asking himself why he did not call her earlier that day, why he did not tell her to stay home, why he did not fly to her city himself. He believes, with a certainty that feels like bone, that he should have been there. That he would have pulled her out of the crowd. That she would still be alive.  

He is not here because he wants to be. His eldest son, a psychologist in another state, called him after a particularly bad week and said, “Dad, you’re not okay. Please talk to someone.” Mr. L. agreed only to stop the phone from ringing. He sits in my office now, his hands folded, his eyes fixed on the window, waiting for permission to leave. He does not believe talking will change anything. He does not believe he deserves to feel better.
